title: Trump Signals Willingness to Work with Democrats to Cap Credit Card Interest Rates at 10%
snippet: President Trump expressed a desire to partner with the incoming Democratic Congress to limit credit card interest rates, reviving an affordability proposal that previously faced opposition from banks and Republicans.
content:
WASHINGTON — In a rare turn toward bipartisan alignment, President Trump announced he is prepared to work with the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress to place a federal cap on credit card interest rates.

"I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump declared during an interview on Fox News Channel's Saturday in America.

The stance re-energizes a key pledge Trump highlighted during his 2024 presidential campaign as part of a broader economic affordability push. The effort previously stalled amid intense pressure from the banking sector and a lack of appetite among congressional Republicans. However, the shift in congressional power appears to have created new momentum for the measure.

A Potential Cross-Aisle Consensus

The central plan under discussion would restrict credit card interest rates to a maximum of 10%. That would represent a steep reduction from current levels. According to Federal Reserve Bank of New York figures, the median credit card interest rate hovering around 22.2%.

Under the 10% proposal, consumer savings would be substantial. A cardholder carrying an average balance of $5,000 currently pays roughly $100 per month strictly in interest charges. With a 10% cap in place, that monthly cost would fall to approximately $42.

The proposal has drawn encouragement from key Democrats, including Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), who is slated to chair the Senate Banking Committee. "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money," Warren said, echoing previous statements that Congress could find common ground with Trump on the issue.

Industry Pushback and Economic Impact

Despite broad consumer appeal, financial institutions have mounted severe opposition to any mandated interest ceiling. Major credit card issuers argue that a 10% rate cap would force them to restrict credit lines, deny approval to lower-income and higher-risk applicants, and significantly curtail popular rewards programs.

However, independent economic research suggests that while bank profit margins would narrow, lenders would remain profitable. Furthermore, researchers estimate that capping rates at 10% could save American consumers roughly $100 billion in interest payments annually.

Data from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau shows that approximately 195 million Americans held credit cards in 2024, paying out $160 billion in interest fees. With total U.S. credit card debt standing at a record $1.23 trillion, proponents argue that statutory intervention is urgently needed to ease financial burdens on working families.
